sam-siegel.title: Samuel Benjamin Siegel
sam-siegel.text: Sources: family testimony from recorded phone calls with his daughter Gloria "Gitty" Siegel and his daughter-in-law Marsha Siegel, both on October 16, 2026, and from his published obituary (Chicago Tribune, September 22, 2009). ## A Chicago furrier Samuel Benjamin Siegel was born July 18, 1913, in Chicago (birth certificate), the second son of Jacob Siegel and Miriam "Mary" Siegel, immigrants from Lespezi, Romania. He grew up in a family of five children: Albert "Al," Sam, Henry "Hank," Morris "Maury," and Pearl, in that order in the 1930 census. On November 17, 1935, in Cook County, he married Anne Greenberg. Their children are Gloria Joy and Jack, born June 25, 1945. Sam worked his whole life in the fur trade. His own shop, Sam Siegel Furs, ended up at 17 North State Street in Chicago. After the shop, he worked part time at Barth Wind Furs on Dempster in Morton Grove and for another furrier on Michigan Avenue whose name the family no longer remembers (Marsha Siegel, October 16, 2026). ## The fur business: two family accounts The family tells the shop's story two ways, and both are kept here. Marsha Siegel, who knew the shop, said Sam was solo, with no partners; his brother Al cut furs at 17 North State on a different floor, and the two were not formally in business together. She placed the shop's later home at 17 North State and thought an earlier location in the Pittsfield Building was possible but was not sure. Gitty Siegel remembered it differently: she said Sam and Al were partners for a time, and that the Pittsfield Building location was "very possible." Wendy Bessinger also believed Sam had partners. The disagreement is recorded as the family holds it; nobody's version has been settled by a document. ## The Tallman house The Siegel family's anchor address was 6550 North Talman Avenue near Devon, the house both Gitty and Jack married from. Earlier homes, per Gitty (October 16, 2026), were around 12th Place and Douglas Boulevard, about 3115 West 15th Street (where Jack was born), and near Congress and Central. The Talman house was a multigenerational one: in the 1950 census, Anne's widowed father, Morris Greenberg, headed a household there that included Sam, Anne, Gloria, Jack, and Anne's half brother Albert "Abe" Greenberg (census record). Morris Greenberg died at that address in 1958 (death record). ## The long life, and the family's heart Sam died in September 2009 at 96. His obituary (Chicago Tribune, September 22, 2009) gives the funeral at Weinstein & Piser in Wilmette and burial at Westlawn Cemetery in Norridge, and names his grandchildren Monte (Cindy), Eric (Tina), Wendy (Paul), and Jennifer (Rich), and great-grandchildren Kailey, Cole, Ross, Carly, and Justin. One small conflict sits in his dates: the Social Security Death Index gives his death as September 21, 2009, while the family's own book records September 20. The tree carries the official record with the family book's date noted.

anne-greenberg-siegel.title: Anne (Greenberg) Siegel
anne-greenberg-siegel.text: Sources: family testimony from a recorded phone call with her daughter Gloria "Gitty" Siegel on October 16, 2026, and Cook County and census records. ## Morris and Esther's daughter Anne Greenberg was born October 19, 1915, in Chicago, the daughter of Morris Greenberg and Esther Moskowitz. Her parents had married in Cook County on October 12, 1912 (marriage record). Anne grew up knowing her father's older children, Minnie and Abe, as her step-sister and step-brother; family testimony held for years that they were children of her father's later remarriage. The records settled it the other way: Minnie and Abe were Morris's children by his first wife, Yetta Unger, so they were Anne's half siblings, and Esther was the second wife. Marsha Siegel confirmed the step-siblings came from the earlier marriage (October 16, 2026), matching the records. ## The Tallman house On November 17, 1935, Anne married Samuel Benjamin Siegel in Cook County. They raised Gloria and Jack (born 1945) in the family home at 6550 North Talman Avenue near Devon, the house both children later married from. It was a crowded, multigenerational house: the 1950 census shows Anne's widowed father Morris heading the household there, with Sam, Anne, Gloria, Jack, and Anne's half brother Abe all under its roof (census record). ## Maury's shadow over the house Anne's brother-in-law Morris "Maury" Siegel, Sam's younger brother, was killed in the Pacific in July 1944, a year before Anne's son Jack was born. The Gold Star mother was Maury's own mother, Miriam Siegel. In the home Anne ran on Talman, Maury's photograph and story stayed present for the next generation; Gitty grew up with her uncle's memory in the house. ## Her death Anne died May 10, 1994, in Chicago and was buried May 12, 1994, at Westlawn Cemetery in Norridge, where Sam would join her in 2009. She was 78. Her grandchildren Monte, Eric, Wendy, and Jennifer are named in Sam's 2009 obituary (Chicago Tribune, September 22, 2009). ## One correction the records made For years, family trees and Ancestry suggestions called Anne's mother "Esther Unger." That was two of Morris's wives merged into one person. Anne's mother was Esther Moskowitz, born 1887 in Piotrkow, Poland, daughter of Vigdor Moskowitz and Gitel (death record). Unger was the maiden name of Morris's first wife, Yetta. The tree now keeps them apart, the way the records do.

jack-siegel.title: Jack Siegel
jack-siegel.text: Sources: family testimony from a recorded phone call with his wife Marsha Siegel on October 16, 2026, and from recorded calls with his sister Gloria "Gitty" Siegel and his daughter Wendy Bessinger the same day. ## Born at 15th Street, married from Talman Jack Siegel was born June 25, 1945, in Chicago, the son of Samuel Benjamin Siegel and Anne (Greenberg) Siegel. He had no middle name; both his wife Marsha and his daughter Wendy confirmed that, and the question is closed. His sister Gitty remembered the family living at about 3115 West 15th Street when he was born; he grew up in the family home at 6550 North Talman Avenue near Devon and married from that house, as Gitty had before him (Gitty Siegel, October 16, 2026). ## Which high school: an open question The family disagrees about Jack's school, and both versions are kept. Marsha said Jack went to Mather High School (Marsha Siegel, October 16, 2026). Gitty said Jack went to Senn. Marsha's account has a detail in its favor: Mather opened in 1959, when Jack was fourteen, so he could have been in its early classes. The conflict is unresolved and marked that way in the tree. ## Cut Rate Toys and Maude Hecht After high school, Jack went to Miami University in Ohio for two years, then came home and attended Mayfair Junior College in Chicago (Marsha Siegel, October 16, 2026). He worked part time at Cut Rate Toys, a toy store on Devon Avenue, and around the time he and Marsha married, the store's owner, Maude Hecht, invited him to become her partner (Marsha Siegel, October 16, 2026). A teenager called "Marky" worked at the store for a few years and was driven there by Jack; whether Marky was Jack's nephew Monte or Mark Machefsky is still an open family question, and a family friend, Tommy Tremel, worked there too (Gitty Siegel, October 16, 2026). ## H&J Liquidators After Wendy went off to college, Jack moved on from the toy business to H&J Liquidators, a closeout and liquidation business, where he worked for the rest of his career (Marsha Siegel, October 16, 2026). ## Marsha, and their daughters Jack married Marsha, born Fern Marsha Baratz. Their daughters are Wendy Ellyn, who married Paul Bessinger, and Jennifer, who married Richard Katin. He died March 12, 2001, at 55, and was buried at Shalom Memorial Park in Arlington Heights (burial record). His father Sam's 2009 obituary names him as "the late Jack (Marsha) Siegel" (Chicago Tribune, September 22, 2009).

jacob-and-miriam-siegel.title: Jacob Siegel and Miriam "Mary" Siegel
jacob-and-miriam-siegel.text: Sources: Cook County birth and death records, the 1930 census, and family testimony from a recorded phone call with their granddaughter Gloria "Gitty" Siegel on October 16, 2026. ## From Lespezi, Romania Jacob Siegel was born about 1889 in Lespezi, Romania (his son Sam's birth certificate spells the town "Lesped," and Jacob's death record gives "Lespiz"; Lespezi, in the Iasi region, is the likely place). His parents were Sam Siegel and Fanny Markovitz (death record). He came to Chicago and worked as a furrier, the trade his sons Albert and Samuel would follow him into. His wife was Miriam, called Mary. Sam's 1913 birth certificate records her as Mary Siegel, 25, born in the same town of Lesped, Romania, as Jacob. Gitty testified that her grandmother Miriam was born a Siegel herself, of an unrelated family (Gitty Siegel, October 16, 2026). That is family testimony, not yet proven: birth indexes often repeat a wife's married name, so the certificate's "Siegel" is consistent with Gitty's account without settling it. Her death, about 1961, has not yet been found in the records. ## Five children, in census order The 1930 census lists Jacob and Mary's children in an order Gitty confirmed from memory exactly (Gitty Siegel, October 16, 2026): Albert "Al" (born about 1911 to 1912, a furrier, who married Lillian Joftus); Samuel Benjamin (born July 18, 1913, who married Anne Greenberg); Henry "Hank" (born December 30, 1914, who married Ethel Lubeznik and moved to California); Morris "Maury" (born June 21, 1919, killed in the Pacific in 1944); and Pearl (born December 21, 1922, who married Abe Machefsky). ## Waldheim, and the First Roumanian Congregation Jacob died September 26, 1941, in Chicago, at about 52, and was buried at Waldheim Cemetery in Forest Park, in the First Roumanian Congregation section. That section became the family's ground: his son Maury was reburied there in 1948 after his death in the war, and Morris Greenberg, the father of Jacob's daughter-in-law Anne, was buried there in 1958. Miriam outlived Jacob by about twenty years, dying about 1961; where she is buried has not yet been confirmed, and finding her record is an open item for the family. She lived long enough to be a Gold Star mother, and her youngest grandchildren grew up in a house where her son Maury's memory was kept.

maury-siegel.title: Morris "Maury" Siegel
maury-siegel.text: Sources: U.S. military and headstone records, and family testimony from a recorded phone call with his sister Gloria "Gitty" Siegel on October 16, 2026. ## The brother who did not come home Morris Siegel, called Maury in the family, was born June 21, 1919, in Chicago, the fourth child of Jacob Siegel and Miriam "Mary" Siegel, between Henry "Hank" and Pearl in the family's 1930 census order. His little sister Gitty remembers him playing with her when she was small, before he left for the war (Gitty Siegel, October 16, 2026). He never married. ## Service and death Maury enlisted on October 23, 1942 (enlistment record, serial 36615896) and served as a Private First Class in Company E, 105th Infantry Regiment, 27th Infantry Division. He was killed on July 9, 1944, in the Pacific. The headstone application does not name the island where he died. His regiment fought on Saipan, and the Battle of Saipan ended on July 9, 1944, the day he died, so he almost certainly died on Saipan; that last step is an inference, labeled as one, not a documented fact. ## The headstone his brother signed After the war, Maury's remains were reburied at Waldheim Cemetery in Forest Park, in the First Roumanian Congregation section, the same section where his father Jacob lies, and where Morris Greenberg, his brother Sam's father-in-law, lies as well. His oldest brother Albert signed the application for his government headstone on July 7, 1948, giving his own address as 1427 West Farwell in Chicago (headstone application card). That signed card is also the document that proves Albert existed under his own name, untangling years of census entries that called him Alex or Abe. ## A Gold Star mother, a flag, and a photograph Maury's mother Miriam became a Gold Star mother. In the family's home his loss was the defining grief of that generation; his sister Gitty spoke of him with pride (Gitty Siegel, October 16, 2026). He is one of two young men in this family who died in service in the Second World War; the other is Harold Kollenberg, a cousin by marriage on the Bessinger side, killed three weeks after Maury, in July 1944.

morris-greenberg.title: Morris Greenberg and his two families
morris-greenberg.text: Sources: England and U.S. census records, Cook County marriage and death records, and family testimony from a recorded phone call with his granddaughter Gloria "Gitty" Siegel on October 16, 2026. ## Romania, then a London locksmith shop Morris Greenberg was born April 15, 1879, in Romania, the son of Alter Greenberg (death record). By the spring of 1901 he was in London, living in St George in the East with his wife Yetta, both recorded as Romanian subjects; the 1901 England census gives his trade as locksmith. Their daughter Mildred "Minnie" was born in London on July 5, 1901, and their son Albert "Abe" followed on December 27, 1902 (or 1903; the records differ by a year). The family crossed to America about 1905. ## The first family, and Yetta's early death In the 1910 census in Chicago's Ward 10, Morris and Yetta appear with Minnie, 8, Abe, 5, and a third child, Tillie, 3, born in Illinois about 1907; Yetta's parents, Israel Unger, 70, born in Romania, and Freeda Unger, 69, born in Poland, lived with them. Tillie is very likely a third child of Morris and Yetta's marriage; she appears in no later family account, and what became of her is one of this family's open questions. Morris's granddaughter Gitty never mentioned her (Gitty Siegel, October 16, 2026); the family is asking Gitty about her before the tree adds her. A Cook County death record for a Yettie Greenberg, who died March 1, 1912, at 32, born in Romania, buried at Forest Park on March 3, 1912, is a strong match for Yetta, though not a certain one: that record names her parents as Saul Unger and Hannah, while the 1910 census puts her parents Israel and Freeda in Morris's own household. If the match holds, Morris was widowed in the spring of 1912 with three small children. ## Esther, and the second family On October 12, 1912, seven months after that death, Morris married Esther Moskowitz in Cook County (marriage record). Esther was born in 1887 in Piotrkow, Poland, the daughter of Vigdor Moskowitz and Gitel (death record). Family stories once said Morris met Esther on the boat; the records say otherwise, since he had arrived in 1905 with Yetta and the children, and married Esther in Chicago seven years later. Morris and Esther's known child is Anne, born October 19, 1915, who married Sam Siegel. Two infant sons of Morris and Esther, born 1913 and 1916, appear in Illinois death and stillbirth records gathered on a shared family tree; they died before they could be part of anyone's memories. Esther died September 6, 1945, in Chicago and was buried the next day at Forest Park. Gitty had anchored Esther's death to "when Jack was a baby"; Jack Siegel was born in June 1945, so her memory and the record agree once her stray "1965 or 66" is set aside as a decade slip. ## Talman Avenue, and the end Morris worked as a machinist. By 1950 the widowed Morris, 72, headed the household at 6550 North Talman Avenue, his son-in-law Sam Siegel's house, living with Sam, Anne, Gloria, Jack, and his son Abe (1950 census). He died February 19, 1958, at that address and was buried February 21 at Waldheim Cemetery in the First Roumanian Congregation section, the same congregation section where Jacob Siegel, his son-in-law Sam's father, and Jacob's son Maury also lie. ## The wider family Morris's brothers, per Gitty (October 16, 2026): Frank Greenberg, "Uncle Frankie," who had a daughter Miriam in Cleveland; and Naftuli Greenberg, whose family died in the camps while he survived, immigrated to America, and lived in New York. Esther's brother was Shmuel, called Samuel, Moskowitz. One warning the records themselves teach: a shared family tree elsewhere gives Morris and Esther a daughter "Sarahann" whose mother is named as an Esther Applebaum. That is a different couple, and the family tree does not copy it.

barban-to-baratz.title: Philip and Mary Baratz: Barban to Baratz
barban-to-baratz.text: Sources: Mary Baratz's 1927 naturalization petition and the SS Lapland passenger manifest of October 1921 (records read in full during the October 16, 2026 research round), with family testimony from recorded calls with Marsha Siegel and Wendy Bessinger on October 16, 2026. ## Pincus and Mirla Philip Baratz was born Pincus Barban on November 5, 1883, in Poland (per Mary Baratz's 1927 naturalization petition). Mary Baratz was born Mirla Barban on July 20, 1890, in Kremnitz, Poland, the town also recorded as Krzemieniec or Kremenets, in historic Volhynia, today western Ukraine (per her 1927 naturalization petition). They married on January 25, 1908, in Poland (per the same petition). Marsha Siegel, their granddaughter, knew her grandmother's maiden name not at all; the records below are how it came back. ## He came first Philip crossed first, alone, sometime before 1921; the exact ship and date of his own arrival are still open. He was naturalized on March 4, 1926, under the name Pincus Barban (per Mary's 1927 naturalization petition, which records his naturalization under that name). Only afterward did the family name in America become Baratz. Nobody at Ellis Island changed it; like so many of these changes, it was made later, in America, by the family itself. ## The Lapland crossing Mary followed with the children in the fall of 1921. Per her 1927 naturalization petition, she emigrated from Antwerp, Belgium, about October 12, 1921, and arrived in New York on October 22, 1921, aboard the SS Lapland, traveling under the name Mirla Barban. The passenger manifest (SS Lapland, sailed Antwerp October 13, 1921, List 5, lines 26 to 28) lists Mirla Barban, 31, wife; Bluma Barban, 12, scholar; and Perce Barban, 9, child; nationality Russian, race Hebrew. Bluma became Bess (Bessie); Perce became Peter. The manifest gives their last residence in a spelling that reads "Siemienic," very likely a misreading of Krzemieniec, and names the nearest relative left behind: "Mother F. Fingerit, Krzemieniec." ## Fingerit: a likely maiden name, held for confirmation That single manifest line is the best evidence of Mary's family name. If the mother left behind in Krzemieniec was F. Fingerit, then Mirla was very likely born Mirla Fingerit. This rests on the manifest entry alone and is marked here as a strong lead, not a settled fact; it is held for family confirmation (Barby Baratz is the family's hope) and for any Krzemieniec record that surfaces. Nothing in the tree depends on it yet. ## Mary signs her new name In 1927, living at 1827 South Hamlin Avenue in Chicago, Mary petitioned for naturalization in the U.S. District Court in Chicago (petition no. 45089). The petition styles her "Mrs. Mary Baratz, formerly Mirla Barban," which is the family's name change caught in a single line of handwriting: Barban in the old country and on the ship, Baratz in Chicago. Their youngest child, Ida, was born in Chicago around 1925, an American from the start. The 1930 census shows the household in Chicago: Philip, Mary, Bessie, Peter, and little Ida, plus a boarder.

peter-baratz.title: Peter Baratz
peter-baratz.text: Sources: family records (SS Lapland passenger manifest, 1921; death record) and recorded phone calls with his daughter Marsha Siegel on October 16, 2026, and with Wendy Bessinger on October 16, 2026. Record facts are cited to the record; family stories are attributed to their teller. ## Perce becomes Peter Peter Baratz was born June 12, 1912, in Poland, the son of Pincus Barban and Mirla Barban, who became Philip and Mary Baratz in America. His given name was Perce (Peretz) Barban. His father came to the United States first; Peter followed with his mother and his older sister Bluma, who became Bess. Per the SS Lapland passenger manifest, the three sailed from Antwerp, Belgium, and arrived in New York on October 22, 1921. Peter was nine years old. His younger sister Ida was born later, in Chicago, around 1925. ## The Poland photograph A studio portrait taken in Poland before the crossing shows young Peter with his sister Bess and their mother Mary. Wendy Bessinger holds the print; the caption on the mount, in Wendy's hand, reads: "Papa Pete (Peter Baratz) with Sister + mom in Poland." Peter looks about eight to eleven in it, which dates it to roughly 1920 to 1923, right around the family's 1921 departure from Antwerp (per Marsha Siegel, recorded call, October 16, 2026, and Wendy Bessinger). A clean scan of the front and back is still to be made; the print itself is a photograph of the original, with inscriptions across the bottom that have not yet been transcribed. ## A working life Peter became a civil engineer for the State of Illinois (per Marsha Siegel, recorded call, October 16, 2026). He married Leah Beberman, daughter of Joseph and Anna Beberman. Their daughters are Marsha, born Fern Marsha Baratz, and Barby Baratz. He died on October 15, 1980, at 68 (death record; Marsha Siegel, recorded call, October 16, 2026). Per the family knowledge base, he is buried at Shalom Memorial Park. ## His sisters Bess, the sister in the Poland photograph, married a Hyman whose first name the family is still trying to pin down. Family lore, told by Marsha (recorded call, October 16, 2026), says Bess's husband invented the Venetian blind and made real money at it; the couple lived in a big colonial house on Chase Street near Sheridan Road, backing onto the beach, and later divorced. Their son Sonny Hyman was wealthy and, by family lore, friendly with Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis; their daughter Arlene is now Simone Simon. Ida, the Chicago-born sister, married Hyman Wicht. ## The brother who was killed: a family story, unproven Wendy Bessinger tells a family story that Peter had a brother who was killed in Europe, in a story involving soldiers coming to the door (per Wendy Bessinger, recorded call, October 16, 2026). Marsha, Peter's own daughter, had never heard this story when asked on her recorded call of October 16, 2026. No record of such a brother has been found, and no name is known. The family's hope for an answer is Peter's daughter Barby Baratz, who holds much of this branch's memory. This story is recorded here as family story only, not as fact, and it stays off the tree until someone or some record can support it.

leah-beberman.title: Leah Beberman
leah-beberman.text: Sources: records (census and death records) and recorded phone calls with her daughter Marsha Siegel on October 16, 2026, and with Wendy Bessinger on October 16, 2026. Record facts are cited to the record; family stories are attributed to their teller. ## Joseph and Anna's daughter Leah Beberman was the daughter of Joseph Beberman and Anna Krecun, Russian-born immigrants whose family arrived in the United States in 1913 (per the 1930 census). Her records give her birth as December 20, 1912, in Illinois and her death as June 4, 1998 (per her death record and the family knowledge base). In census records she also appears as "Lena," the kind of name shortening that runs all through this family. She married Peter Baratz, the civil engineer, himself an immigrant who had crossed as a nine-year-old named Perce Barban. Their daughters are Marsha, born Fern Marsha Baratz, and Barby Baratz. ## Her brothers and sisters Leah's siblings, as the family and the records together give them: Fanny, called Faye, who married Emil A. Jacobson and whose son Edward "Eddie" Jacobson (records and family testimony agree); Theodore, called Ted; and William, called Will, a cook for Walgreens who died young, when Marsha was a small child (per Marsha Siegel, recorded call, October 16, 2026). Whether William and Theodore were two brothers or one man under two names is an open question, taken up in Joseph and Anna's story document; it is unresolved. ## The Wicht and Hyman connections Leah's family braided into Peter's through his sisters. Peter's younger sister Ida Baratz married Hyman Wicht, so Ida was Leah's sister-in-law. Peter's older sister Bess married a Hyman whose first name is still unknown to the family; family lore credits him with inventing the Venetian blind and making real money, and their son Sonny Hyman and daughter Arlene, now Simone Simon, are Leah's niece and nephew by marriage (family lore via Marsha Siegel, recorded call, October 16, 2026; Ida's obituary in the Chicago Tribune, March 9, 2011, also names Arlene and Simon among the family). ## The birth date wrinkle: unresolved Leah's dates do not sit comfortably together. Her death record and family records say she was born December 20, 1912, in Illinois. But if the Bebermans arrived in 1913, a daughter born in Illinois in December 1912 cannot fit, and the 1930 census ages her at about 14, which points to a birth around 1915 or 1916 in Illinois (per the 1930 census). One of these is wrong; the likeliest check is her Social Security record (the NUMIDENT file), which has not been pulled yet. Her date is carried in the tree as the records give it, and the conflict is marked unresolved here rather than smoothed over.

joseph-and-anna-beberman.title: Joseph and Anna Beberman
joseph-and-anna-beberman.text: Sources: records (censuses, death records, Find a Grave) and recorded phone calls with Marsha Siegel and Wendy Bessinger on October 16, 2026, plus Wendy Bessinger's phone note shared October 16, 2026. Record facts are cited to the record; family stories are attributed to their teller, and unproven material is marked as such. ## Arrival, 1913 Joseph Beberman was born February 15, 1880, in Russia, and Anna, whose maiden name the records give as Krecun (Marsha has also heard it as "Krekon"), was born December 18, 1884, in Russia (per their death records; both rest at Westlawn Cemetery). The 1930 census shows the family arrived in the United States in 1913. They settled in Chicago, and the household the censuses catch over the years holds the whole next generation: Fanny, Leah, Theodore, and, depending on which record you read, William. ## The children Fanny, born about 1912 in Russia, so an infant on the crossing, married Emil A. Jacobson; the family called her Faye. Her son is Edward "Eddie" Jacobson (records; Marsha Siegel, recorded call, October 16, 2026). Leah, who married Peter Baratz, has her own story document. Theodore, called Ted, was born October 15, 1914, and died December 8, 1986. ## William versus Theodore: unresolved The family also remembers a William Beberman, "Uncle Will," a cook for Walgreens who died young, while Marsha was a small child (per Marsha Siegel, recorded call, October 16, 2026). Wendy Bessinger names William among Leah's brothers too, and says she herself may be named for Grandma Leah's brother William (per Wendy Bessinger, recorded call, October 16, 2026). The records complicate it: a 1950 census shows a William Beberman born in 1914 "At Sea," which fits a birth during the family's 1913 to 1914 crossing, but the tree already carries Theodore Joseph Beberman, born October 15, 1914, and two babies in one year is unlikely unless they were twins. William and Theodore may be two brothers, or one man remembered and recorded under two names. William is held out of the tree pending an answer, and Marsha and Barby are the people to ask. Marked unresolved. ## Max Beberman: the family's famous mathematician Wendy's phone note puts it plainly: "Joseph Beberman brother was ??? Brothers son max beberman." The brother's name is the hole in the note; nobody living knows it. But the nephew's story is family canon. Max Beberman (born August 20, 1925, in Brooklyn; died January 24, 1971, in London) directed the University of Illinois Committee on School Mathematics, the UICSM, and was a towering figure of the "New Math" movement; the New York Times carried his obituary on January 26, 1971. Marsha confirmed the family story on her recorded call of October 16, 2026: Max was the mathematician, he was at the University of Illinois, Barby Baratz told the story first,. So: the family story is confirmed by Marsha, and the famous Max fits the note's generation exactly (a nephew of Joseph, born in the 1920s). The identity on paper is still marked unproven: no record yet names the famous Max's father, and until a birth record, obituary, or university file names him, the link rests on family testimony. Barby, the story's source, knows the whole of it and is the family's living authority.

samuel-schatzman.title: Samuel Schatzman
samuel-schatzman.text: Sources: family records and the Schatzman / Bessinger research project, October 2026. Samuel's death facts are from his 1919 Cook County death record. The passages about his wife and daughters are marked where they rest on leads rather than proof. ## The patriarch we know least Samuel Schatzman was born in 1864 in Drashna, Russia, a son of Moshe Itzhok Schatzman. He brought his family to Chicago, and his son Ancil grew up to found a grocery wholesale business and anchor the family's American story. Samuel himself barely outlived the crossing generation: he died on November 23, 1919, at his home at 2454 Walton Street, Chicago, and was buried the next day at Jewish Waldheim Cemetery in Forest Park. His death certificate is the anchor record for this whole branch of the family, and it is nearly all we have of him so far. ## The open question of his wife Who Samuel's wife was is an OPEN question, and the story document keeps it that way. His 1919 death certificate names his wife as Ida. The 1910 census shows his wife as "Fennie." A member tree researched by Katharine Williams, whose Fuegi-Williams tree overlaps this family heavily, gives his wife as Eva Ovensky, born about 1862 in Russia, who appears as a widowed head of household in the 1920 census with a daughter Ida, and who died July 18, 1922, in Chicago. Eva may be the same woman as an "Eva Omansky" Ancestry once suggested for Ancil's mother. One woman under three names, or more than one marriage, is not yet resolved; the records have been asked for, and nothing here should be read as settled. ## Daughter leads, not yet proven The same member tree gives Samuel three daughters, and each is a LEAD pending a death record that names Samuel as father. Anna Schatzman married Isaac Itsig Rubenstein, called Ruby, in 1908; she died October 19, 1918, in Chicago, leaving children Marshall, David, and Florence, and she may be the very link that connects Katharine Williams to this family. Rose Schatzman married Meyer Dorne and died November 3, 1949, in Chicago; Samuel's Find a Grave entry independently names a daughter "Rose Dorne," which makes her the strongest of the three leads. Ida Schatzman, born about 1893 in Russia, never married, lived with Eva in 1920, and died February 12, 1949, in Chicago. If the death records confirm them, Samuel's story gains a whole second household. ## Notes for the family Samuel's arrival record, his own parents' story in Drashna, and the fate of a possible daughter named Ella all remain unfound. What is solid: a man from Drashna, a Walton Street home, a Waldheim grave, and a son who built Mid-City Wholesale Grocers.

ancil-and-sophie-schatzman.title: Ancil and Sophie Schatzman
ancil-and-sophie-schatzman.text: Sources: family records and the Schatzman / Bessinger research project, October 2026. Ancil's career and funeral details are from his 1978 Chicago newspaper obituary clipping, saved in the project sources. Record facts are cited to the records named in the text. ## Ancil and Mid-City Ancil Schatzman was born in Drashna, Russia, a son of Samuel Schatzman. His birth date comes down in three versions: his death record says August 15, 1893, his naturalization record says December 25, 1892, and a Social Security record says December 25, 1890. He came to Chicago as a boy and built his life in the grocery business. His 1978 obituary calls him a founder and former executive of Mid-City Wholesale Grocers, where he worked for more than 50 years before retiring about ten years before his death. He died on August 24, 1978, at Weiss Memorial Hospital, living at the end at the Northwest Home for the Aged on North California Avenue. His services were held at Congregation Rodfei Zedek in Hyde Park, the family congregation. ## Sophie of Mogilev Sophie Edelson was born in Mogilev, in what is now Belarus, in August 1895; her death record gives August 21, her naturalization petition August 23, and Social Security August 24. Her parents were Jacob Edelson of Mogilev and Eva Shapotkin. The family arrived in New York on September 4, 1903, sailing from Bremen, when Sophie was eight. Records also show Edelson siblings for her, Isadore, Elizabeth "Betty" Plavnik, and Emily Chelin, whose stories are still being recovered. Sophie married Ancil in Chicago on June 21, 1914. She died on August 2, 1975, and was buried at Waldheim Cemetery in Forest Park. ## Their children Marvin, the oldest, was born March 19, 1915, and followed his father into groceries before going into banking. Walter, born in March 1919, died on November 3, 1924, at age five, and was buried at Waldheim; for years the family story remembered only that a sibling had died young, and the records gave Walter back his name. Janet, born June 23, 1921, married Milton Rappeport and died April 12, 1972. Vivian, born December 1, 1925, married Dr. Paul Schutz and later Richard Handel, and lived to 98. Ancil's obituary names his survivors as his son Marvin, his daughter Mrs. Vivian Handel, five grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren; Janet had died six years before him. ## Notes for the family Ancil's three birth dates stay in the record as found; no single one is proven. An ashtray with "ANCIL" written on it, kept by his granddaughter Barbara, is still in the family today, a small piece of him.

marvin-schatzman.title: Marvin Schatzman
marvin-schatzman.text: Sources: family records and the Schatzman / Bessinger research project, October 2026. Marvin's banking role is stated in his father Ancil's 1978 newspaper obituary. ## From groceries to the bank chairman's office Marvin Eugene Schatzman was born March 19, 1915, in Chicago, the oldest child of Ancil and Sophie Schatzman. He followed his father into Mid-City Wholesale Grocers, then made a second career in banking. By the time of his father's death in 1978, Marvin was chairman of Republic Bank of Chicago, which is how Ancil's obituary introduces him to the world: the grocer's son, named first among the survivors, running a bank. He lived a long life, dying January 23, 2009, at 93. ## Marriage and family Marvin married Ruth Levin, born March 30, 1921, a daughter of Irving Levin and Etta Nathan. Their daughter Barbara Ann, born July 22, 1944, married Robert John Bessinger, tying the Schatzman and Bessinger lines together in the generation above Ross. Marvin was, by every account the project has gathered, the senior figure of his generation: when his little brother Walter died in 1924 at age five, Marvin was nine, old enough to remember, and the memory of a sibling lost young survived in the family through him. Ruth outlived him by eight years, dying February 17, 2017; she is buried in Skokie. ## Notes for the family Marvin's own obituary and a fuller account of his years at Republic Bank are still worth pulling; his story here leans on his father's obituary and the family's records. His granddaughter Barbara kept family keepsakes, including an ashtray marked with his father's name, Ancil, that survives in his great-grandson's family today.

vivian-schatzman.title: Vivian Schatzman
vivian-schatzman.text: Sources: family records and the Schatzman research project, October 2026. Paul Bessinger's naming is per his wife Wendy, on a recorded call on October 16, 2026. The history session passage is a family lead, marked as sought where it appears. ## The youngest, and the longest lived Vivian Schatzman was born December 1, 1925, in Chicago, the youngest child of Ancil and Sophie Schatzman. She outlived everyone in her generation of the family, dying June 19, 2024, at 98. When her father died in 1978, his obituary listed her as Mrs. Vivian Handel, a daughter among the survivors; she had another forty-six years still to live. ## Two marriages, and a namesake Vivian married first Dr. Paul Schutz; their sons are Ronald and Charles Schutz. She married second Richard Handel. The Schutz marriage left a mark on the wider family that is still in use: her nephew Robert Bessinger named his son Paul after Dr. Paul Schutz (per Wendy Bessinger, recorded call, October 16, 2026). So the Paul who carries this whole project forward in the present generation carries Dr. Schutz's name with him. ## The keeper of the history Late in her life, Vivian sat with her cousin Marcia Katin, who hosted her for what the family calls "a whole history thing," a session where Vivian walked through the family's past. The family believes a VIDEO of that session may exist: Marcia may still have it, Paul may have it, and the family is asking. It is the project's most wanted artifact, marked here as sought, not found. If it surfaces, Vivian's own voice becomes the narrator of half the stories in this set, which is exactly what she seems to have intended.

irving-and-etta-levin.title: Irving and Etta Levin
irving-and-etta-levin.text: Sources: family records and the Levin research project, October 2026. Dates and burials are from death records, burial records, and the Ancestry hint sweep of October 2026. Etta's mother's identity is an open conflict and is marked as such. ## Irving Irving Levin was born March 9, 1897, in Chicago, a son of Max H. Levin and Fannie Bernstein. Max had come from Russia, born December 15, 1877, and died January 7, 1924, in Chicago; he was buried at Waldheim. Fannie, by the consistent set of records found in the 2026 hint sweep, died September 30, 1970. Irving died May 8, 1975, and was buried the next day at Westlawn Cemetery in Norridge. ## Etta of O'Brien Street Etta Nathan was born October 26, 1896, at 75 O'Brien Street, Chicago, an address preserved on her birth record and matched exactly by an independent member tree. Her father was Barnett Nathan, born about 1870 in Russia, who died, by the records found in the sweep, on January 24, 1939. Her mother was Anna Greenberg. The tree long carried her maiden name as Polishuk, but Etta's birth certificate and her parents' January 8, 1893 Cook County marriage record give the name as Annie Greenberg or Greenburg, no record supports Polishuk, and Ross settled it as Greenberg on Oct 19, 2026. Anna, by the sweep's records, was born December 16, 1873, and died in late May 1943. Member trees give Etta siblings Bertha, David, Bessie, Isadore Irving, and Lillian; those are leads, not yet on this tree. ## Their family Irving and Etta married on August 17, 1919, in Chicago. Their daughters were Ruth, born March 30, 1921, who married Marvin Schatzman, and Marilyn, born May 28, 1927, who married Jack Kornick. Etta died September 26, 1978, and was buried at Westlawn beside Irving. Between them they stand at the crossing of two of this family's main lines: their granddaughter Barbara Schatzman married Robert Bessinger, and their grandson-in-law Jack Kornick's family fills its own story in this set.

marilyn-and-jack-kornick.title: Marilyn and Jack Kornick
marilyn-and-jack-kornick.text: Sources: family records and the Levin research project, October 2026. Marilyn's funeral and burial are from her Chicago Tribune death notice of December 1, 2008. The trust case passage is from the published federal opinion named in the text. ## Sixty-one years Marilyn Harriet Levin was born May 28, 1927, in Chicago, the younger daughter of Irving Levin and Etta Nathan. She married Jack Kornick, and they stayed married for over 61 years, as her death notice puts it, a span that carried them from the 1940s to 2008. Marilyn died November 30, 2008. Her service was held December 2, 2008, at the Weinstein Funeral Home North Shore Chapel in Wilmette, and she was interred at Memorial Park Cemetery in Skokie, the same cemetery where her sister Ruth rests. ## Jack and the carpet business Jack Kornick was born April 17, 1925, in Chicago, and built his working life in the carpet business, running Jack Kornick & Associates. He was a son of Ben H. Kornick and Fanny Kornick, and the brother of Irving Kornick and of Lorraine, who married Hyman Spreckman. Jack died July 25, 2014, six years after Marilyn. Their sons were Barry Kornick (January 27, 1949 to December 19, 2025) and Randi Kornick. ## The trust case, a public record curiosity The Kornick name survives in one unusual place: a published federal court opinion, Schatzman v. Talley (91 F.R.D. 270), about the Ben H. Kornick Trust, in which Fanny Kornick was the income beneficiary and Jack, Irving, and Lorraine appear as Ben's children. It is a dry document, but it confirms the family's shape from an unexpected direction, and it ties this story to the Schatzmans by name as well as by marriage. It is noted here as a curiosity of the public record, not as family lore.

leopold-bessinger.title: Leopold Bessinger
leopold-bessinger.text: Sources: family records and the Bessinger research project, October 2026. Leopold's own account of his birth and arrival is from his 1937 naturalization petition, read as an image by the project. Edith's parentage is from her 1974 Cook County death record. ## A child immigrant from Stuttgart Leopold Bessinger was born in Stuttgart, Germany, on June 1, and even the year is his to argue with: his Social Security record says 1883, while in his own naturalization petition, sworn in 1937, he stated 1886. What the petition settles is the outline. He arrived in New York in 1887 as a small child, traveling under the name Leopold Bissinger, and he grew up to work as a salesman of knit goods in Chicago, living at 943 East 52nd Street in Hyde Park. He waited a long time to become a citizen, naturalizing on November 18, 1937, fifty years after he landed. ## Marriage and family On February 27, 1913, in Chicago, Leopold married Edith Todd Brown. Edith was a Chicago-born daughter of David Brown and Rose Kohn, Bohemian Jewish families whose Chicago story is still being recovered; she died May 19, 1974, and was buried at Graceland Cemetery. Leopold and Edith had three children: Ralph, born July 15, 1915; and the twins Herbert and Ruth Janet, born February 9, 1920. Leopold died in April 1966 and was buried in Chicago on April 22 of that year. ## Notes for the family The 1883 versus 1886 birth year is recorded both ways and flagged wherever it appears; his petition statement is the more personal source, the Social Security record the earlier claim, and no document yet ends the argument. How a Stuttgart child named Bissinger became a Chicago Bessinger is, so far, the whole story of the surname in America: spelled one way on the ship, another way in the life he built.

ralph-and-sybil.title: Ralph and Sybil Bessinger
ralph-and-sybil.text: Sources: family records and the Bessinger research project, October 2026. Marriage details are from the Cook County marriage index. The Burger funeral page passage is a lead, marked as unproven where it appears. ## Ralph Ralph Joseph Bessinger was born in Chicago on July 15, 1915, the oldest child of Leopold and Edith Bessinger. A small record quirk follows him: his birth certificate and the Social Security death index say July 15, while his draft card, his Social Security claims file, and public records say July 16. The birth certificate, written closest to the event, is the one the family record keeps. Ralph died September 5, 1995, in Chicago. ## Sybil of St. Louis Sybil Minnette Burger was born May 12, 1914, in St. Louis, Missouri, a daughter of John S. Burger and Jennie M. Ebeling, who had married in Bellwood, Illinois, in 1909. Her family name is written Burger in the records; the Social Security Administration carried a variant, Boger, which the family record notes and sets aside. She had a brother, Samuel Burger. The Burger side is the thinnest branch of this tree: Sybil's generation is nearly all we have of it so far. ## Their family Ralph and Sybil married on August 12, 1938, in Cook County. Their son Robert John was born April 2, 1943. Their daughter Barbara Ann, called Barbara A. to keep her distinct from her Schatzman cousin of nearly the same name, was born October 20, 1945; she never married and died June 9, 1975, at 29. Sybil lived to December 22, 2000. Ross Bessinger, Robert's grandson, is named after Ralph (per Ross, October 2026), which is why the name Ralph anchors this branch. ## The Burger branch: an unproven lead In April 2026 a Chicago Jewish Funerals page for John Steven Burger (January 3, 1943 to April 21, 2026), a son of Stanley and Ruth Burger, reached Paul Bessinger from a relative who had sought the family out. This is a LEAD, not a fact: if Stanley Burger was another son of John S. Burger and Jennie Ebeling, he would be Sybil's brother, and John Steven Burger her nephew. The timeline fits and no record yet proves or breaks it; John Steven Burger's Cook County birth record, which should name his parents, is the test the project has queued. Until it lands, the Burger branch stays as Sybil left it: St. Louis born, Chicago married, and mostly still to be found.

herbert-bessinger.title: Dr. Herbert Bessinger
herbert-bessinger.text: Sources: family records and the Bessinger research project, October 2026. Herbert's career details are from his 2006 Chicago Tribune obituary (Legacy id 2461313). The section on his wife is an open question and is marked as such. ## The doctor Dr. Herbert Edwin Bessinger was born February 9, 1920, in Chicago, a twin with his sister Ruth Janet, and a son of Leopold and Edith Bessinger. He earned his medical degree at the University of Illinois, served in the U.S. Army, and joined the staff of Weiss Memorial Hospital in 1958. He stayed thirty years, until 1988, and built much of the institution he served: he founded its internal medicine residency program and created its first intensive care unit, twenty beds, at the time the largest in Chicago. The hospital's Herbert Bessinger Award of Excellence is named for him. He died May 20, 2006. His Tribune obituary names no wife, no funeral home, and no cemetery, which is part of why the question below exists. ## His family Herbert's children are Donald Bessinger and Lois Bessinger Dee, known from his obituary and the family record. His twin Ruth married Harold Grinker; her children were Janet, Susan, and David. When Ruth died in May 2004, her Tribune notice named her as the sister of Dr. Herbert Bessinger, the two twins still paired in print at the end. ## The open question: Herbert's wife Who Herbert married is the biggest open question on the Bessinger side, and this document states it plainly rather than guessing. The leads, all unproven: a Cook County marriage record dated July 31, 1942, found among his Ancestry hints and not yet pulled as an image; a flagged 1950 census household in Kentucky showing Herbert with a wife and a child; and a Social Security claims record that gives his birth year as 1918 against 1920 everywhere else. The 1942 marriage record is the decisive document, and it is queued. Family memory may beat the records to it: his nephew Paul is being asked directly, and anything he remembers will be added here with his name on it.

robert-and-barbara-bessinger.title: Robert and Barbara Bessinger
robert-and-barbara-bessinger.text: Sources: family records and the Bessinger / Schatzman research project, October 2026. The ashtray detail is per Wendy Bessinger, on a recorded call on October 16, 2026. This story is deliberately short: it says what is known and names what is not. ## What the record holds Robert John Bessinger was born April 2, 1943, in Chicago, a son of Ralph and Sybil Bessinger. Barbara Ann Schatzman was born July 22, 1944, a daughter of Marvin Schatzman and Ruth Levin. They married, and their son is Paul Andrew Bessinger. Robert died December 24, 2003. Barbara died May 13, 2020. That is the whole of the documentary record the project has assembled for them so far, and it is thinner than it should be for the couple at the center of this family's living memory. ## What is still open Robert's occupation, whether he served in the military, and where he is buried are open questions, and they are being put directly to Paul, who is being interviewed for this project; whatever he adds will be written here with his name on it. A yahrzeit list at Congregation Beth Shalom of Northbrook names a Robert Bessinger alongside Sybil, which is a lead toward his burial, not a confirmation. ## The ashtray One object carries Barbara's care for this family's history better than any document. In the family home sits an ashtray with the name "ANCIL" written on it, Ancil Schatzman being Barbara's grandfather. Barbara kept it, and it has stayed in the family. His mother's keepsake of her grandfather is still in the house, waiting for its photograph to join the project sources.
